questions.stem: A tracheal biopsy from a 43-year-old smoker shows stratified squamous epithelium where pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium is expected. Which statement best describes this change?
questions.explanation: Metaplasia is a reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type by another that better tolerates chronic stress; squamous epithelium resists smoke but sacrifices mucociliary function. A: Dysplasia is disordered growth with atypia, not replacement by another normal cell type. C: Hyperplasia increases cell number without changing cell type. D: Metaplasia is reversible if the stimulus is removed. E: Atrophy is shrinkage, not a change of cell type.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p2; tutorial s19, s22

questions.stem: After an acetaminophen overdose, which finding indicates that hepatocytes have crossed into irreversible injury?

options.C: Membrane blebs with loss of microvilli
options.D: Leakage of AST and ALT into blood

questions.explanation: Loss of plasma membrane integrity lets intracellular enzymes leak into the blood: a hallmark of irreversible injury (along with pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis). A: Swelling and ER dilation reflect ion-pump failure and are reversible. B: Fatty change is reversible. C: Blebs form while the membrane is still intact (reversible). E: Chromatin clumping is reversible; pyknosis, karyorrhexis and karyolysis are irreversible.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p4; tutorial s26–30

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man dies 3 weeks after a large stroke. The infarcted area of brain is soft and cystic. Which pattern of necrosis is this?
questions.explanation: Ischemic injury in the CNS produces liquefactive necrosis: tissue is digested into a soft mass that later becomes a cyst. A: Coagulative necrosis is typical of ischemia in other solid organs. B: Caseous necrosis is seen in TB granulomas. D: Fibrinoid necrosis affects vessel walls. E: Fat necrosis occurs in pancreatitis and breast.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p5; tutorial s43

questions.stem: Which feature favors apoptosis over necrosis?

options.A: Apoptotic bodies cleared with little inflammation
options.D: Death of large groups of adjacent cells
options.E: Leakage of cell contents into the blood

questions.explanation: Apoptosis: shrinkage, intact membrane, apoptotic bodies rapidly phagocytosed with minimal inflammation, usually single cells or small clusters. B: Swelling and rupture are necrosis. C: This nuclear sequence (ending in karyolysis) is listed for necrosis; apoptosis shows chromatin condensation and fragmentation. D: Necrosis often affects groups of adjacent cells. E: Leakage of contents is necrosis.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p6–7; tutorial s46

questions.stem: Coronary flow is restored by angioplasty 4 hours after occlusion, but serum troponin rises further and some still-viable myocytes die. Which mechanism best explains this?

options.B: Fatty change from impaired lipid metabolism
options.E: Reperfusion injury from ROS and calcium overload

questions.explanation: Restoring flow to still-viable ischemic tissue can worsen injury: more ROS, calcium overload, inflammation, and complement activation. A: Growth-factor withdrawal isn't the trigger here. B: Fatty change is a reversible accumulation, not a cause of cell death. C: There is no infection; pyroptosis is an inflammasome response to microbes. D: Calcification follows necrosis; it doesn't cause it.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p4; tutorial s40

questions.stem: A lymph node biopsy shows back-to-back follicles. Immunostaining shows strong BCL-2 in the follicle centers, and a t(14;18) translocation is found. What is the effect of BCL-2 overexpression?

options.B: Promotes cytochrome c release from mitochondria

questions.explanation: BCL-2 opposes BAX/BAK, preventing cytochrome c release and intrinsic apoptosis, so B cells survive and accumulate (follicular lymphoma). A: Caspase-8 belongs to the extrinsic (death-receptor) pathway. B: BCL-2 prevents cytochrome c release. D: BCL-2 doesn't activate p53. E: MLKL is activated by RIPK1/RIPK3 in necroptosis.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p6; tutorial s45

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has acute epigastric pain radiating to the back and elevated lipase. At surgery, chalky white deposits are seen in the peripancreatic fat. What process produced them?

options.E: Saponification of fatty acids with calcium

questions.explanation: Enzymatic fat necrosis: pancreatic lipases release fatty acids that bind calcium (saponification), giving chalky white deposits. A: Caseous necrosis is TB. B: Metastatic calcification needs hypercalcemia and occurs in normal tissue. C: Acinar necrosis doesn't produce chalky deposits in fat. D: Fibrinoid necrosis affects vessel walls.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p5; tutorial s48–49

questions.stem: In a macrophage infected with bacteria, inflammasome activation triggers caspase-1, which cleaves gasdermin D. Pores form, the cell swells and ruptures, and IL-1β is released. Which form of cell death is this?
questions.explanation: Pyroptosis: inflammasome → caspase-1 → gasdermin D pores, swelling and rupture; caspase-1 also activates IL-1β and IL-18. A: Necroptosis uses RIPK1/RIPK3 → MLKL. C: Ferroptosis is iron-dependent lipid peroxidation when glutathione-GPX4 defenses fail. D: Apoptosis keeps the membrane intact with little inflammation. E: Autophagy is mainly a survival response.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p7; tutorial s33–34

questions.stem: A 65-year-old with long-standing aortic stenosis has a thick-walled left ventricle. Which change explains the myocardial enlargement?

options.B: Replacement of myocytes by a more resistant cell type
options.C: Disordered myocyte growth with nuclear atypia
options.D: Larger myocytes from more structural proteins and organelles

questions.explanation: Cardiac myocytes have limited capacity to divide, so pressure overload causes hypertrophy: increased synthesis of structural proteins and organelles. A: Hyperplasia requires cells that can divide. B: That is metaplasia. C: That is dysplasia. E: That is fatty change, a form of reversible injury.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p1; tutorial s5–6
